weiner-2016.gazette: The crew filming Weiner's 2013 run for New York mayor had a key to the office rather than a spot on the press line — co-director Josh Kriegman had worked for him in Congress. What that access produced is the campaign as it actually ran: staff meetings, car rides, the phone going off, the second scandal breaking from inside the frame. The record of the primary and the footage of it are the same thing.

120-bpm-beats-per-minute-2017.gazette: Robin Campillo sat in ACT UP Paris's weekly general meetings before he ever staged one, and the film runs on that procedure — snapping fingers instead of applause, points of order, votes taken while people are dying. The zaps, the die-ins, the fake blood thrown across pharmaceutical offices follow actions the group carried out in the early 1990s. It plays like a movement's own minutes, read back at speed.

dunkirk-2017.gazette: Operation Dynamo ran from late May into early June 1940 and lifted more than 330,000 men off the French coast, much of it from a single stone breakwater never built to berth ships. Nolan shot on the real beach and split the film along the clocks the evacuation actually kept: a week on the mole, a day at sea, an hour of fuel in the air. The geography does the arithmetic.
dunkirk-2017.prism: Running three clocks at once is faithful to the operation and merciless to the men inside it — the soldier waiting a week and the pilot with an hour of fuel were never living in the same event. That accuracy has a price: nobody in the film is ever allowed to see the rescue whole.

god-s-own-country-2017.gazette: Francis Lee grew up on a Yorkshire hill farm, and the film keeps the work at its own speed — lambing, walling, the skinning of a dead lamb so its fleece can be tied onto an orphan the ewe will then accept. The actors were sent out to farms before the shoot rather than coached on set. It is the contract British realism has held since Loach: the labour is filmed as labour, and the people are filmed around it.

i-am-not-your-negro-2017.gazette: Baldwin left about thirty pages of a book called Remember This House, about three men he knew — Medgar Evers, Malcolm X, Martin Luther King Jr. — killed within five years of one another. Raoul Peck built the film from those pages and archival footage, writing no narration of his own. Every line spoken over the images is Baldwin's.

i-tonya-2017.gazette: The screenplay came out of separate interviews with Tonya Harding and Jeff Gillooly, whose accounts of the same marriage and the same 1994 attack failed to match anywhere it mattered. Rather than choose a version, the film shoots several and lets the characters break frame to dispute the scene they are standing in. The testimony stays contradictory on screen because it stayed contradictory on the record.
i-tonya-2017.prism: Filming every version keeps faith with the documents and quietly hands the audience a job the courts never finished. Harding gets the benefit of the doubt as a technique rather than a verdict — and Kerrigan, who was struck and had no competing story to tell, nearly vanishes from her own case.

loveless-2017.gazette: Russia's volunteer search organisations — Liza Alert and groups like it — work where the police decline to, walking grid lines through woods and derelict buildings with flyers and megaphones. Zvyagintsev films the procedure as it actually runs: the intake questions, the sectors assigned, the ruined hotel cleared floor by floor. The volunteers are the only people in the film who do their job.

the-death-of-stalin-2017.gazette: Stalin collapsed at his dacha on the night of 1 March 1953 and lay on the floor for hours because nobody was willing to open the door. Moscow's senior physicians were in prison at the time, swept up in the Doctors' Plot, so the Presidium sent for whoever remained. Iannucci compresses the months that followed, Beria's arrest and execution among them, but keeps the names, the offices and the order of events.

the-disaster-artist-2017.gazette: Wiseau shot The Room in 2002 on 35mm and HD simultaneously, using cameras he bought outright instead of renting, and spent a reported six million dollars that has never been fully accounted for. Franco follows Greg Sestero's memoir through that production — the water-bottle rig, the alley set built beside a real alley, the line reset dozens of times. The events are documented; only the money isn't.
the-disaster-artist-2017.prism: A film about a man who could not tell how he was being received, made by people who knew exactly how they would be. The affection is genuine and it is also the safest available position — the failure has been converted into an asset, and Wiseau is the only person who was ever exposed by it.

the-lost-city-of-z-2017.gazette: Fawcett's expeditions began as border survey work for the Royal Geographical Society in 1906 and turned into a twenty-year search for a ruined city the Society treated as fantasy. He disappeared into the Amazon in 1925 with his eldest son, and rescue parties have been disappearing after him ever since. James Gray works from David Grann's account and Fawcett's own diaries, which stop where the record does.

3-faces-2018.gazette: Panahi has been under a filmmaking ban in Iran since 2010 and appears here as precisely that: a director working from the front seat of a car he is not permitted to be working from. The retired actress living at the edge of the village stands in for Shahrzad, a star of pre-revolutionary Iranian cinema written out of the industry after 1979 and left in obscurity. The camera never goes inside her house.

an-elephant-sitting-still-2018.gazette: The film was shot in the Hebei rustbelt in winter, in cities that thinned out as the state plants wound down. Hu Bo holds almost every scene in a single long take with a shallow focus that keeps the background legible and unreachable, and never lights his way out of the grey. Four hours, one day, one bus leaving town.
an-elephant-sitting-still-2018.prism: The unbroken take is a claim: nothing has been cut away, so nothing can be blamed on the edit. It also means the audience serves the same four hours the characters do — the film's honesty and its cruelty are the identical technique.

asako-i-ii-2018.gazette: Hamaguchi rehearses by having actors read the script aloud without expression, again and again, until inflection stops arriving out of habit — a method he takes from Renoir and worked out on Happy Hour with non-professionals. That flatness survives into the finished performances, which is why the film's least plausible turns are played at room temperature. The 2011 earthquake arrives in the middle of it, filmed the same way.

ash-is-purest-white-2018.gazette: The middle stretch is set in the Three Gorges as the water came up, in towns being taken apart by hand ahead of the flood that displaced well over a million people. Jia had filmed those same streets years earlier, before they went; parts of what is on screen now exist at no elevation at all. The dam kept its schedule.

blackkklansman-2018.gazette: Ron Stallworth ran the Colorado Springs Klan investigation by telephone in the late 1970s while a white colleague attended the meetings under his name. His memoir supplies the calls with David Duke and the membership card that came in the mail; Lee composites the partner and invents his Jewish background. The film closes on footage from Charlottesville, shot forty years later and left uncut.
blackkklansman-2018.prism: The invented partner is the tell — the real case carried no interior conflict, so the film manufactured one to have something to argue with. The closing footage then does the opposite of period work: it withdraws the past tense the whole movie had been filmed in.
